label: eq:3
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A continuous function $\Phi$, defined on the positively invariant subset of $\Omega$, under consideration, is called a Lyapunov function for system \eqref{eq:5} if, along every trajectory $(x(t),y(t))$ in this subset, the finite limit
\[
\lim_{t\to+\infty}\Phi(x(t),y(t))
\]
exists.
head: environment

label: eq:6
title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $n<\nu$. Then
\[
\Phi(x,y)=\prod_{j=n+1}^{\nu}y_j
\]
is a Lyapunov function for system \eqref{eq:5}.

If $b_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j=n+1}^{\nu}b_j=1$, then
\[
\Phi_b(x,y)=\prod_{j=n+1}^{\nu}y_j^{b_j}
\]
is also a Lyapunov function; factors with $b_j=0$ are not taken into account. If
\[
\mu_b=\min_{1\le k\le n}\sum_{j=n+1}^{\nu}b_jq_{kj}>0,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:6}
\Phi_b(x,y)\le \Phi_b(x^0,y^0)e^{-\mu_b t}.
\end{equation}
If
\[
\mu_{0j}=\min_{1\le k\le n}q_{kj}>0,\qquad j=n+1,\ldots,\nu,
\]
then
\[
y_j\le y_j^0e^{-\mu_{0j}t}
\]
and
\[
\omega(x^0,y^0)\subset S^{n-1}\times\Upsilon,
\qquad
\Upsilon=\{y\in S^{\nu-1}:y_{n+1}=\cdots=y_{\nu}=0\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $j>n$,
\[
\dot y_j=-y_j\sum_{k=1}^n q_{kj}x_k\le0.
\]
Hence $y_j$, and with it $\Phi(x,y)$, is non-increasing and bounded below by zero.

If $y_j>0$ for every $j$ with $b_j>0$, then
\[
\frac{\dot\Phi_b}{\Phi_b}
=-\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\sum_{j=n+1}^{\nu}b_jq_{kj}\le-\mu_b.
\]
If one of the factors involved is initially zero, it remains zero and $\Phi_b\equiv0$. Inequality \eqref{eq:6} follows from Gr\"onwall's lemma. The coordinatewise estimates are obtained analogously and give the stated inclusion for the $\omega$-limit set.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $n=\nu$, $1\le r<n$ and
\[
p_{jk,j}^{(f)}+p_{jk,j}^{(m)}<1,\qquad
p_{kj,j}^{(f)}+p_{kj,j}^{(m)}<1
\]
for $1\le j\le r<k\le n$. Then
\[
\Phi(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}(x_j+y_j)
\]
is a Lyapunov function. If
\[
\Phi_0=\Phi(x^0,y^0)<2
\]
and
\[
\vartheta=
\min_{\substack{1\le j\le r\\r<k\le n}}
\left\{1-p_{jk,j}^{(f)}-p_{jk,j}^{(m)},\,
1-p_{kj,j}^{(f)}-p_{kj,j}^{(m)}\right\}>0,
\]
then
\[
\Phi(x,y)\le \Phi_0e^{-\vartheta(1-\Phi_0/2)t}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $X=\sum_{j=1}^r x_j$, $Y=\sum_{j=1}^r y_j$, then
\[
\dot\Phi\le-\vartheta[X(1-Y)+Y(1-X)]
\le-\vartheta\Phi\left(1-\frac{\Phi_0}{2}\right).
\]
Since $\Phi_0<2$ this gives the required exponential estimate.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Suppose there exist $l\in\{n+1,\ldots,\nu\}$, $q\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that
\[
\max_{1\le i\le n}p_{il,l}^{(m)}
\le
\min_{1\le k\le\nu}p_{qk,q}^{(f)}.
\]
Then, on the relative interior of $\Omega$,
\[
\Phi(x,y)=\frac{y_l}{x_q}
\]
is a Lyapunov function.

If
\[
\vartheta_1=
\min_{1\le k\le\nu}p_{qk,q}^{(f)}-
\max_{1\le i\le n}p_{il,l}^{(m)}>0,
\]
then
\[
\dot\Phi<0,\qquad \Phi(x,y)\le\Phi_0e^{-\vartheta_1t}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The logarithmic derivative satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln\Phi
\le
\max_{1\le i\le n}p_{il,l}^{(m)}-
\min_{1\le k\le\nu}p_{qk,q}^{(f)}.
\]
The non-strict condition guarantees that $\Phi$, does not increase, while the strict condition gives its exponential decay.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $a_qc_q<b_qd_q$. If $n<\nu$ assume in addition $\varepsilon_q>0$. Then
\[
\Phi_q(x,y)=(1-x_q)+\varrho_q(1-y_q)
\]
is a Lyapunov function relative to $E_q$. The equilibrium $E_q$ is locally exponentially asymptotically stable, and
\[
\mathcal{A}(E_q)=\Omega\setminus\Upsilon_q.
\]
Since $\operatorname{codim}_{\Omega}\Upsilon_q=2$, the equilibrium $E_q$ is almost globally asymptotically stable: its basin of attraction $\mathcal{A}(E_q)$ has full measure in $\Omega$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on the affine hull of $\Omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put
\[
u=1-x_q,\qquad
v=\sum_{\substack{l=1\\l\ne q}}^n y_l,\qquad
w=\sum_{l=n+1}^{\nu}y_l,
\]
where, when $n=\nu$, $w=0$. Then $\Phi_q=0$ only at $E_q$.

From system \eqref{eq:5}, using the stochastic and Volterra conditions, we obtain
\[
\dot u\le a_qx_qv-b_qy_qu.
\]
For $n<\nu$,
\[
\dot w\le-\varepsilon_qx_qw-T_q,
\qquad
\dot v\le c_qy_qu-d_qx_qv+T_q,
\]
where
\[
T_q=\sum_{\substack{i=1\\i\ne q}}^n\sum_{l=n+1}^{\nu}
\left(1-p_{il,l}^{(m)}\right)x_i y_l.
\]
For $n=\nu$ the term $T_q$ is absent from the estimate for $\dot v$.

Since
\[
b_q-\varrho_qc_q=\varrho_qd_q-a_q=\gamma_q,
\]
we have
\[
\dot\Phi_q\le-\gamma_qy_qu-\gamma_qx_qv-\varrho_q\varepsilon_qx_qw\le0,
\]
where, for $n=\nu$, the last term is absent.

Choose a neighborhood of $E_q$, in which $x_q\ge\delta$ and $y_q\ge\delta$ for some $\delta>0$, and then a sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ so that the set $\{\Phi_q\le\varepsilon\}$ is contained in this neighborhood. This set is positively invariant, and on it
\[
\dot\Phi_q\le-\gamma_0\Phi_q,
\]
where
\[
\gamma_0=\delta\min\left\{\gamma_q,\frac{\gamma_q}{\varrho_q},\varepsilon_q\right\}\quad(n<\nu),
\]
and at $n=\nu$,
\[
\gamma_0=\delta\min\left\{\gamma_q,\frac{\gamma_q}{\varrho_q}\right\}.
\]
Since $\Phi_q$ is equivalent to the distance to $E_q$ on $\Omega$, this estimate proves local exponential stability.

From the global estimate for $\dot\Phi_q$ it follows that $\dot\Phi_q<0$ outside $\{E_q\}\cup\Upsilon_q$. On $\Upsilon_q$,
\[
\Phi_q=1+\varrho_q,
\]
and $\Upsilon_q$ is positively invariant.

If $(x^0,y^0)\notin\Upsilon_q$, then
\[
\Phi_q(x^0,y^0)<1+\varrho_q,
\]
so the monotonicity of $\Phi_q$ rules out any $\omega$-limit set with $\Upsilon_q$. By LaSalle's invariance principle,
\[
(x,y)\to E_q\qquad\text{as }t\to+\infty.
\]
Hence $\mathcal{A}(E_q)=\Omega\setminus\Upsilon_q$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
The equilibrium $E_q$ is locally exponentially asymptotically stable relative to $\Omega$ if and only if
\[
\Delta_{qi}>0\qquad\text{for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{q\},
\]
and, if $n<\nu$, $\varepsilon_q>0$.

If $\Delta_{qi}<0$ for at least one $i\ne q$, then $E_q$ is unstable. If $\Delta_{qi}=0$ for at least one $i\ne q$ or if $n<\nu$, $\varepsilon_q=0$, then $E_q$ is non-isolated and is not asymptotically stable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After eliminating the dependent coordinates $x_q,y_q$ the reduced Jacobian of system \eqref{eq:5} has two-dimensional blocks
\[
J_{qi}^{(5)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-A_{qi}&B_{qi}\\
C_{qi}&-D_{qi}
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where, for $i\ne q$,
\[
A_{qi}=p_{iq,q}^{(f)},\qquad
B_{qi}=1-p_{qi,q}^{(f)},\qquad
C_{qi}=1-p_{iq,q}^{(m)},\qquad
D_{qi}=p_{qi,q}^{(m)},
\]
with $0\le A_{qi},B_{qi},C_{qi},D_{qi}\le1$. For $n<\nu$ there are additional one-dimensional blocks
\[
-p_{ql,q}^{(m)},\qquad l>n.
\]
The block structure of the reduced Jacobian together with the Hurwitz criterion ensures local exponential asymptotic stability whenever the conditions of the first part of the lemma hold. If $\Delta_{qi}<0$, the corresponding block has a positive eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector, so small perturbations along that eigenvector remain within the invariant face $\Omega_{qi}$, proving instability of $E_q$.

At $\Delta_{qi}=0$ the equilibrium equations on $\Omega_{qi}$ written in the variables $x_i/x_q$, $y_i/y_q$ form a homogeneous linear system with a nonzero nonnegative solution. Consequently, at $\Delta_{qi}=0$ there exist equilibria in $\Omega$ that accumulate at $E_q$. Food $n<\nu$ and $\varepsilon_q=0$ the segment of states with a single female type $q$ and male types $q,l$, where $l>n$ and $p_{ql,q}^{(m)}=0$, consists entirely of equilibria. In both cases $E_q$ is non-isolated, so asymptotic stability is impossible.
head: environment

label: eq:7
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Volterra condition preserves the vanishing coordinates outside $I_1$, while the equality $A_1^{(f)}=A_1^{(m)}=A_1$ ensures the invariance of the diagonal $x_i=y_i=s_i$. Hence \eqref{eq:7} holds on $\Omega_1$.

The skew-symmetry of $A_1$ preserves $\sum_{i\in I_1}s_i=1$, and the equations preserve the positivity of the $s_i$; hence, $\Omega_1$ is invariant.

Since $A_1$ is skew-symmetric with $\operatorname{rank} A_1=2$, there exist linearly independent $u,v$, for which
\[
A_1=uv^T-vu^T.
\]
Then
\[
s_i(t)=s_i^0e^{u_i\alpha(t)+v_i\beta(t)},
\]
where
\[
\dot\alpha(t)=Z_\beta(\alpha(t),\beta(t)),\qquad
\dot\beta(t)=-Z_\alpha(\alpha(t),\beta(t)),\qquad
\alpha(0)=\beta(0)=0,
\]
and
\[
Z(\alpha,\beta)=\sum_{i\in I_1}s_i^0e^{u_i\alpha+v_i\beta}.
\]
Hence $Z(\alpha(t),\beta(t))\equiv1$.

From $C\in\ker A_1$, $C_i>0$ it follows that $0$ lies in the interior of the convex hull of the vectors $(u_i,v_i)$. Hence $Z$ is strictly convex and coercive. From $A_1s^0\ne0$ it follows that $\nabla Z(0,0)\ne0$, so $\min Z<1$. Therefore the level set $Z=1$ is a regular simple closed curve. The Hamiltonian vector field does not vanish on it, so motion along this level set is periodic. Consequently, the trajectory $s(t)$ is periodic, and the condition $A_1s^0\ne0$ rules out a constant solution.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: For any $N_0\ge3$ and $0<\theta\le1$ and any $I_1\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N_0\}$, there exists a VQSOBP with $n=\nu=N_0$, such that all interior non-equilibrium trajectories of its continuous analogue on $\Omega_1$ are periodic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\bar q\in\{f,m\}$ and $1\le i<j\le N_0$ put
\[
p_{ij,i}^{(\bar q)}=p_{ji,i}^{(\bar q)}
=\frac12\left(1+\theta\sin\frac{2\pi(j-i)}{N_0}\right),
\]
\[
p_{ij,j}^{(\bar q)}=p_{ji,j}^{(\bar q)}
=\frac12\left(1-\theta\sin\frac{2\pi(j-i)}{N_0}\right).
\]
Put the diagonal coefficients equal to one and all others equal to zero. A direct check shows that these coefficients satisfy the stochastic and Volterra conditions, and $A_1^{(f)}=A_1^{(m)}=A_1$. The matrix $A_1$ is skew-symmetric, has rank $2$, and
\[
(1,1,\ldots,1)^T\in\ker A_1.
\]
Hence all the conditions of Lemma~6 are satisfied, and the assertion follows from it.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Systems of the form \eqref{eq:7} with a skew-symmetric matrix $A_1$ have previously been studied, in particular in \cite{ref41}, where, under corresponding conditions on $\ker A_1$, periodicity of interior non-equilibrium trajectories was established. The corollary above provides an explicit realization of such a mechanism within the continuous analogue of the VQSOBP for every $N_0$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $n=\nu=3$. For each $\bar q\in\{f,m\}$ and each cyclic pair $(i,j)=(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)$ put
\[
p_{ij,i}^{(\bar q)}=p_{ji,i}^{(\bar q)}=\frac34,\qquad
p_{ij,j}^{(\bar q)}=p_{ji,j}^{(\bar q)}=\frac14.
\]
For pairs of parents with identical indices, the heredity coefficient of the matching type is set to one, and all remaining coefficients not specified above are set to zero. Then
\[
A_1=\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&-1\\
-1&0&1\\
1&-1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{rank} A_1=2,\qquad
\ker A_1=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)\}.
\]
For
\[
x(0)=y(0)=s^0=\left(\frac12,\frac13,\frac16\right)
\]
we have $A_1s^0\ne0$, and on $\Omega_1$ system \eqref{eq:5} takes the form
\[
\begin{cases}
\dot s_1=s_1(s_2-s_3)/2,\\
\dot s_2=s_2(s_3-s_1)/2,\\
\dot s_3=s_3(s_1-s_2)/2.
\end{cases}
\]
By Lemma~6 the corresponding trajectory is periodic. A numerical computation of its period gives $T\approx23.17873$. Figure~\ref{fig:periodic} shows projections of this trajectory onto the planes $(s_1,s_2)$ and $(s_2,s_3)$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{figure1.png}
\caption{Projections of the periodic trajectory onto the planes $(s_1,s_2)$ and $(s_2,s_3)$.}
\label{fig:periodic}
\end{figure}

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For fixed $i\ne q$ when $\Delta_{qi}>0$ the characteristic equation of the block $J_{qi}^{(5)}$ has two real negative roots $\lambda$, and the corresponding eigenvalues of the block
\[
J_{qi}^{(4)}=I_2+J_{qi}^{(5)},
\]
where $I_2$ is the identity matrix of order two, equal $\mu=1+\lambda$.

All roots satisfy $\lambda\ge-2$, with equality possible only when $A_{qi}=B_{qi}=C_{qi}=D_{qi}=1$, i.e., when $\Delta_{qi}=0$. Hence, when $\Delta_{qi}>0$, both roots satisfy
\[
-2<\lambda_{1,2}<0,\qquad -1<\mu_{1,2}=1+\lambda_{1,2}<1.
\]
If $\Delta_{qi}<0$, one of the roots $\lambda$ is positive, so $\mu>1$. If $\Delta_{qi}=0$ then
\[
\lambda_1=0,\qquad \mu_1=1,
\]
and the second root equals
\[
\lambda_2=-(A_{qi}+D_{qi}),\qquad \mu_2=1-A_{qi}-D_{qi}.
\]
For the additional coordinates $y_l$, $l>n$, the eigenvalues of the one-dimensional blocks of the reduced Jacobian matrices of system \eqref{eq:5} and of $W$ equal, respectively,
\[
-p_{ql,q}^{(m)},\qquad 1-p_{ql,q}^{(m)}.
\]
This proves the hyperbolicity criterion. When $\Delta_{qi}>0$ for all $i\ne q$ and, if $n<\nu$, $\varepsilon_q>0$, then, by the theorem on stability by first approximation, the point $E_q$ is locally exponentially asymptotically stable both for system \eqref{eq:5} and for $W$.

If $\Delta_{qi}<0$, the eigenvector of the block $J_{qi}^{(5)}$ corresponding to the positive eigenvalue $\lambda$, can be chosen with positive coordinates (see Lemma~5). The corresponding direction is admissible on the invariant two-type face $\Omega_{qi}$, and for the operator $W$ this same eigenvector corresponds to an eigenvalue $\mu>1$. Hence $E_q$ is unstable relative to $\Omega$ both for $W$, and for system \eqref{eq:5}.

If $\Delta_{qi}=0$ for at least one $i\ne q$ or, when $n<\nu$, $\varepsilon_q=0$, then by Lemma~5 the point $E_q$ is non-isolated and is not asymptotically stable. This proves $3^\circ$. Taking into account the case $\Delta_{qi}<0$ we obtain the necessity of the conditions $\Delta_{qi}>0$ for all $i\ne q$ and, when $n<\nu$, $\varepsilon_q>0$ in $2^\circ$.

title: Remark
body_md: In the non-hyperbolic case, when $\Delta_{qi}\ge0$ for all $i\ne q$ Lemma 7 Lemma~7 does not allow one to judge the Lyapunov stability of $E_q$ or its preservation under the transition from $W$ to system \eqref{eq:5}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=$\arabic*^\circ$.,leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Let, for a fixed $q\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
\[
\left(1-p_{qi,q}^{(f)}\right)\left(1-p_{jq,q}^{(m)}\right)
<p_{jq,q}^{(f)}p_{qi,q}^{(m)},
\qquad i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{q\},
\]
where $i=j$ is allowed, and when $n<\nu$, $\varepsilon_q>0$. Then
\[
\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{disk}}(E_q)=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{cont}}(E_q)=\Omega\setminus\Upsilon_q,
\]
with
\[
\omega_{\mathrm{disk}}(z^0)=\omega_{\mathrm{cont}}(z^0)=\{E_q\}
\qquad\text{for all }z^0\in\Omega\setminus\Upsilon_q.
\]
\item For any $q,i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $q\ne i$, the equality
\[
\omega_{\mathrm{disk}}(z^0)=\omega_{\mathrm{cont}}(z^0)
\]
holds for all $z^0\in\Omega_{qi}$ if and only if
\[
\left(p_{iq,q}^{(f)},p_{qi,q}^{(f)},p_{iq,q}^{(m)},p_{qi,q}^{(m)}\right)\ne(1,0,0,1).
\]
When this condition holds, both trajectories with a common initial state converge to the same equilibrium. If $\Delta_{qi}>0$, the common limit equals $E_q$ for all $z^0\in\Omega_{qi}\setminus\{E_i\}$; if $\Delta_{qi}<0$, it equals $E_i$ for all $z^0\in\Omega_{qi}\setminus\{E_q\}$. For the excluded coefficient set, the equality $\omega_{\mathrm{disk}}(z^0)=\omega_{\mathrm{cont}}(z^0)$ holds precisely when $x_i^0=y_i^0$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By virtue of the conditions o $1^\circ$ for some $\rho>0$ the function
\[
L_q=(1-x_q)+\rho(1-y_q)
\]
does not increase for $W$ and system \eqref{eq:5}, and strictly decreases outside $\{E_q\}\cup\Upsilon_q$. Since its maximum is attained exactly on $\Upsilon_q$, for $z^0\notin\Upsilon_q$ the monotonicity excludes limit points on this face. By the invariance principle for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5}, both $\omega$-limit sets equal $\{E_q\}$. Since $\Upsilon_q$ is closed, invariant, and does not contain $E_q$, we obtain the stated equality of the basins of attraction.

On the two-type face $\Omega_{qi}$, the condition of $1^\circ$ is equivalent to $\Delta_{qi}>0$, and $\Upsilon_q\cap\Omega_{qi}=\{E_i\}$. Hence, when $\Delta_{qi}>0$ both trajectories converge to $E_q$ for all initial states except $E_i$. If $\Delta_{qi}<0$, then $\Delta_{iq}=-\Delta_{qi}>0$, and both trajectories converge to $E_i$ for all initial states except $E_q$.

Let $\Delta_{qi}=0$ and
\[
\left(p_{iq,q}^{(f)},p_{qi,q}^{(f)},p_{iq,q}^{(m)},p_{qi,q}^{(m)}\right)\ne(1,0,0,1).
\]
In cases where one of the coordinates is constant, the equation for the other coordinate becomes linear, and the corresponding discrete map becomes affine; the coefficient of the varying coordinate in the discrete map lies in the interval $[0,1]$; if it equals unity, both trajectories are stationary. Therefore, the continuous and discrete trajectories share the same limit.

Let
\[
p_{iq,q}^{(f)}=0,\qquad p_{iq,q}^{(m)}=1,\qquad
p_{qi,q}^{(f)}<1,\qquad p_{qi,q}^{(m)}>0,
\]
then the function
\[
H_1=p_{qi,q}^{(m)}x_i+\left(1-p_{qi,q}^{(f)}\right)y_i
\]
is a common first integral for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5}. The coordinate $x_i$ is non-decreasing, $y_i$ is non-increasing, and on each level segment of $H_1$ the equilibrium is unique. Hence both trajectories converge to the same equilibrium.

In the remaining cases $A_{qi},C_{qi}>0$, and the common first integral
\[
H_2=\left(1-p_{iq,q}^{(m)}\right)x_i+p_{iq,q}^{(f)}y_i
\]
defines invariant segments, on each of which the equilibrium is unique. After eliminating one coordinate using the condition $H_2=\operatorname{const}$ the discrete dynamics reduces to a one-dimensional map $T$, for which $|T'(u)|<1$ at interior points of the segment. Hence the distance to the equilibrium strictly decreases, and, by compactness of the segment, the discrete trajectory converges to it. The continuous trajectory on the same segment tends monotonically to this equilibrium. Single-point levels consist of equilibria. Consequently, the continuous and discrete trajectories converge to the same equilibrium.

For the excluded coefficient set, the discrete trajectory on $\Omega_{qi}$ forms a two-cycle when $x_i^0\ne y_i^0$, while the continuous trajectory converges to the equilibrium
\[
x_i=y_i=\frac{x_i^0+y_i^0}{2}.
\]
Consequently, in this case $\omega_{\mathrm{disk}}(z^0)=\omega_{\mathrm{cont}}(z^0)$ if and only if $x_i^0=y_i^0$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=$\arabic*^\circ$.,leftmargin=2.4em]
\item If $\Gamma$ is a non-constant periodic orbit of system \eqref{eq:5}, then $W(\Gamma)\nsubseteq\Gamma$.
\item On $\Omega_{qi}$ there are no non-constant periodic orbits of system \eqref{eq:5}. Non-constant cycles of $W$ exist precisely for the coefficient set excluded in $2^\circ$ of Lemma~8. All of them have minimal period $2$.
\item Let $A_1^{(f)}=A_1^{(m)}=:A_1$. Then on $\Omega_1$ the operator $W$ has no non-constant cycles. For the existence of an interior non-constant periodic trajectory of system \eqref{eq:5} on $\Omega_1$ it is necessary that
\[
\ker A_1\cap(0,\infty)^{|I_1|}\ne\varnothing.
\]
If $\operatorname{rank} A_1=2$, this condition is also sufficient, and all interior non-equilibrium trajectories of system \eqref{eq:5} on $\Omega_1$ are periodic.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At the point $z^*\in\Gamma$, where the Euclidean norm attains its maximum, we have
\[
\langle z^*,F(z^*)\rangle=0,\qquad F(z^*)\ne0,
\]
where $F$ is the right-hand side of system \eqref{eq:5}. Hence
\[
\|W(z^*)\|^2=\|z^*\|^2+\|F(z^*)\|^2>\|z^*\|^2,
\]
which proves $1^\circ$.

Item $2^\circ$ follows directly from item $2^\circ$ of Lemma~8.

Invariance of $\Omega_1$ for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5} is equivalent to the equality $A_1^{(f)}=A_1^{(m)}=A_1$.

Suppose a discrete cycle exists. Taking the logarithm of the coordinate equalities and summing them over the period, using the inequality $\ln(1+\xi)\le\xi$ we obtain $A_1\bar s\ge0$, where $\bar s>0$ is the average over the cycle. Since $A_1$ is skew-symmetric, $\bar s^TA_1\bar s=0$, so $A_1\bar s=0$. Consequently, equality is attained in all the logarithmic inequalities used, and every point of the cycle is fixed.

For a continuous periodic trajectory, averaging the equations
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln s_i=(A_1s)_i
\]
over a period shows that its positive average belongs to $\ker A_1$. Therefore, the condition
\[
\ker A_1\cap(0,\infty)^{|I_1|}\ne\varnothing
\]
is necessary for any rank of $A_1$. When $\operatorname{rank} A_1=2$ the sufficiency of this condition and the periodicity of all non-equilibrium trajectories on $\Omega_1$ follow from Lemma~6.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Despite the coincidence of the fixed points of the operator $W$ and the equilibria of system \eqref{eq:5}, their periodic regimes generally differ. On a two-type face, a discrete two-cycle may fail to persist under the transition to the continuous analogue, whereas on $\Omega_1$ system \eqref{eq:5} may possess non-constant periodic trajectories in the absence of non-constant cycles of the operator $W$.
head: environment

label: eq:8
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:8}
\left(1-p_{qi,q}^{(f)}\right)\left(1-p_{jq,q}^{(m)}\right)
<p_{jq,q}^{(f)}p_{qi,q}^{(m)},
\qquad 1\le q<n,\quad q<i,j\le n,
\end{equation}
where $i=j$ is allowed, and, when $n<\nu$, additionally
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:9}
\varepsilon_q>0,\qquad q=1,\ldots,n.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}W^k(z^0)=\lim_{t\to+\infty}z(t;z^0)=E_q,
\qquad
\omega_{\mathrm{disk}}(z^0)=\omega_{\mathrm{cont}}(z^0)=\{E_q\}.
\]
The fixed points of the operator $W$ and the equilibria of system \eqref{eq:5} are exhausted by $E_1,\ldots,E_n$, and, for each $q=1,\ldots,n$,
\[
\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{disk}}(E_q)=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{cont}}(E_q)
=\{z\in\Omega:x_i=y_i=0\ (i<q),\ x_q+y_q>0\}.
\]
All points $E_q$ are hyperbolic for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5}. The dimensions of the unstable and stable spectral subspaces of the reduced Jacobian matrices at $E_q$ equal, respectively, $q-1$ and $n+\nu-q-1$.

Relative to $\Omega$ the point $E_1$ is locally exponentially asymptotically stable, while the points $E_q$, $q>1$, are unstable both for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5}. There are no non-constant cycles of the operator $W$ and no periodic orbits of system \eqref{eq:5} on
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $z^0\in\Omega$ and the corresponding index $q$. By the Volterra condition, the face defined by the equalities $x_i=y_i=0$ for $i<q$, is invariant for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5}. For $q<n$, after eliminating the absent types, conditions \eqref{eq:8}, \eqref{eq:9} ensure that the conditions of $1^\circ$ of Lemma~8 hold for the restriction to this face. Since $x_q^0+y_q^0>0$, both $\omega$-limit sets equal $\{E_q\}\{E_q\}$; compactness of $\Omega$ gives convergence of both trajectories to $E_q$.

For $q=n$ on the face under consideration $x_n=1$. If $n<\nu$, then for $l>n$,
\[
y_l^{(k+1)}=\left(1-p_{nl,n}^{(m)}\right)y_l^{(k)}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\dot y_l=-p_{nl,n}^{(m)}y_l.
\]
From \eqref{eq:9} it follows that $y_l\to0$ as $k\to+\infty$, whence $y_n\to1$. When $n=\nu$ this face consists of $E_n$.

Consequently, the formula for the common limit is established for all initial states. It determines the stated basins of attraction; its application to constant trajectories rules out other fixed points and equilibria. Convergence of all trajectories to equilibria rules out non-constant periodic regimes.

Let now $q\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be arbitrary. Applying \eqref{eq:8} with $i=j$ and using $\Delta_{qi}=-\Delta_{iq}$, we obtain
\[
\Delta_{qi}>0\quad(i>q),\qquad \Delta_{qi}<0\quad(i<q).
\]
Consequently, taking \eqref{eq:9} into account, by Lemma~7 all $E_q$ are hyperbolic for $W$ and for system \eqref{eq:5}; $E_1$ is locally exponentially asymptotically stable, while $E_q$, $q>1$, are unstable relative to $\Omega$.

Each $i<q$ corresponds to exactly one unstable eigenvalue of each of the two reduced Jacobian matrices, while the remaining eigenvalues are stable. Hence the dimension of the unstable spectral subspace equals $q-1$. Since the order of each reduced matrix equals $n+\nu-2$, the dimension of the stable spectral subspace equals $n+\nu-q-1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The class of VQSOBPs satisfying the conditions of Theorem~1 is non-empty. Choose $a_0,b_0\in(0,1)$ so that $a_0+b_0>1$, and, for every pair of parents with distinct indices $i,j\le n$ set the probability of inheriting the smaller index equal to $a_0$ for female offspring and $b_0$ for male offspring. If $n<\nu$ additionally put
\[
p_{ql,q}^{(m)}=c_0\in(0,1),\qquad 1\le q\le n<l\le\nu.
\]
The remaining coefficients are determined by the stochastic and Volterra conditions. Then all conditions of Theorem~1 are satisfied.
head: environment

label: eq:15
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:17
title: Proof
body_md:
From \eqref{eq:12} and \eqref{eq:14} we have
\[
M_1\le\mu M_0^2,\qquad
M_k\le\upsilon M_{k-1}+\mu\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}M_iM_{k-1-i},\qquad k\ge2.
\]
For
\[
A_L=\sum_{k=0}^L M_k,\qquad L\ge1,
\]
we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:17}
A_L\le(1-\upsilon)M_0+\upsilon A_{L-1}+\mu A_{L-1}^2.
\end{equation}
For $\mu>0$ put
\[
V^*=\frac{1-\upsilon-\sqrt{(1-\upsilon)^2-4\mu(1-\upsilon)M_0}}{2\mu}.
\]
Condition \eqref{eq:15} ensures the reality of $V^*$, and
\[
M_0\le V^*,\qquad
(1-\upsilon)M_0+\upsilon V^*+\mu(V^*)^2=V^*.
\]
Since the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:17} is non-decreasing in $A_{L-1}$, induction gives $A_L\le V^*$ for all $L$. For $\mu=0$ all $v_k$, $k\ge1$, equal to zero. Thus,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}M_k<\infty,
\]
and series \eqref{eq:16} converges absolutely and uniformly.

Summing the recurrence relations \eqref{eq:14} over $k$ and using the absolute convergence of the series, we obtain an integral equation equivalent to problem \eqref{eq:11}. Hence the sum of series \eqref{eq:16} is a solution of problem \eqref{eq:10}. Uniqueness follows from the local Lipschitz continuity of the polynomial mapping $F_1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For $-2<\hbar<0$ condition \eqref{eq:15} is equivalent to
\[
4KC_BM_0\le g(\hbar),\qquad
g(\hbar)=
\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{2+\hbar}{\hbar},&-2<\hbar<-1,\\[1ex]
1,&-1\le\hbar<0.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence values of $\hbar$ from the interval $[-1,0)$ give, within this criterion, the least restrictive sufficient condition
\[
4KC_BM_0\le1.
\]
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $J$ be a Hurwitz matrix with Jordan data $\{\lambda_i,h_i\}_{i=1}^N$. Then for every $k\ge0$ the term $v_k(t,\hbar)$ of series \eqref{eq:16} has the form
\[
v_k(t,\hbar)=\sum_{s=1}^N\sum_{\lambda\in S_k}\sum_{l=0}^{P_k}
C_{s,l,\lambda}^{(k)}t^le^{\lambda t}e_s,
\]
where
\[
S_k=\{\lambda_{i_1}+\cdots+\lambda_{i_r}:1\le r\le k+1\},
\qquad i_1,\ldots,i_r\in\{1,\ldots,N\},
\]
and
\[
P_k\le h_{\max}+k(2h_{\max}+1),\qquad
h_{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le N}h_i.
\]
The coefficients $C_{s,l,\lambda}^{(k)}$ pare determined recurrently by the quantities $a_{0i},\lambda_i,h_i,b_{ij}^{s}$ and $\hbar$.

If the matrix $J$ is diagonalizable and its eigenvalues are real, negative, and linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, then $C_{s,l,\lambda}^{(k)}=0$, for $l\ge1$, i.e., each $v_k(t,\hbar)$ is a finite sum of exponentials.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The assertion follows by induction on $k$ from \eqref{eq:14}. Under quadratic convolution, the exponents of the exponentials and the degrees of the polynomial factors add, while the action of the Duhamel operator augments the set of possible exponents by the eigenvalues of $J$ and increases the maximal degree of the polynomial factor by at most $h_{\max}+1$. This gives the stated $S_k$ and the estimate for $P_k$. In the diagonalizable case, linear independence of the eigenvalues over $\mathbb{Q}$ excludes resonances, so polynomial factors do not arise in subsequent terms either.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the Cauchy problem for the continuous analogue of $W_9$ \cite{ref10}:
\[
\begin{cases}
\dot x_1=y_1-x_1,\\
\dot x_2=y_2-x_2,\\
\dot y_1=x_1y_2,\\
\dot y_2=x_2y_2-y_2,
\end{cases}
\qquad
(x_1(0),x_2(0),y_1(0),y_2(0))=(x_1^0,x_2^0,y_1^0,y_2^0)\in\Omega_2,
\]
for which no solution in quadratures was obtained in \cite{ref26}.

Eliminating $x_2=1-x_1$ and $y_2=1-y_1$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:20}
\begin{cases}
\dot x_1=y_1-x_1,\\
\dot y_1=x_1(1-y_1),
\end{cases}
\qquad
(x_1(0),y_1(0))=(x_1^0,y_1^0).
\end{equation}
Its equilibria are $(0,0)$ -- a hyperbolic saddle, and $(1,1)$ -- an asymptotically stable improper node.

Set $u=x_1-1$, $v=y_1-1$. Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:21}
\begin{cases}
\dot u=v-u,\\
\dot v=-uv-v,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
and, since $v=\dot u+u$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:22}
\ddot u+2\dot u+u\dot u+u+u^2=0,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:23}
u(0)=u_0,\qquad \dot u(0)=v_0-u_0.
\end{equation}
The stationary solutions are $u\equiv0$ and $u\equiv-1$. For $v_0=0$ the trajectory lies on the invariant line $v=0$, and
\[
u(t)=u_0e^{-t}.
\]

Consider now the more general problem
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:24}
\ddot u+2\dot u+u=f(u,\dot u),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:25}
u(0)=u_0,\qquad \dot u(0)=v_0-u_0,
\end{equation}
where it is assumed that for $|U|<r_1$, $|V|<r_2$ the function $f$ admits the absolutely convergent power series representation
\[
f(U,V)=\sum_{\mathfrak n,\mathfrak m\ge0}a_{\mathfrak n,\mathfrak m}U^{\mathfrak n}V^{\mathfrak m},
\qquad a_{\mathfrak n,\mathfrak m}\in\mathbb{R},
\]
where $0<r_1,r_2\le+\infty$.

Set
\[
\mathcal{N}_1[u]=\ddot u+2\dot u+u-f(u,\dot u),
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_1[\varphi]=\ddot\varphi+2\dot\varphi+\varphi.
\]
The solution of the problem $\mathcal{L}_1[\varphi]=g$ with initial conditions \eqref{eq:25} has the form
\[
\varphi(t)=(u_0+v_0t)e^{-t}+\int_0^t(t-\tau)e^{-(t-\tau)}g(\tau)\,d\tau.
\]
For zero initial data and a bounded continuous function $g$, the estimates
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:26}
\|\varphi\|_\infty\le\|g\|_\infty,
\qquad
\|\dot\varphi\|_\infty\le2\|g\|_\infty
\end{equation}
hold.

For $\hbar\ne0$ introduce the deformation equation
\[
(1-p)\mathcal{L}_1[U]=\hbar p\mathcal{N}_1[U],
\]
\[
U(0,p,\hbar)=u_0,\qquad \dot U(0,p,\hbar)=v_0-u_0.
\]
We seek the solution as a formal series
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:27}
U(t,p,\hbar)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}u^{[k]}(t,\hbar)p^k,
\qquad
u^{[k]}=\left.\frac{1}{k!}\frac{\partial^kU}{\partial p^k}\right|_{p=0}.
\end{equation}
Here
\[
u^{[0]}(t)=(u_0+v_0t)e^{-t},
\qquad
u^{[k]}(0,\hbar)=\dot u^{[k]}(0,\hbar)=0,\quad k\ge1.
\]
Let
\[
f(U,\dot U)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}F^{[k]}(t,\hbar)p^k.
\]
Comparing coefficients of like powers of $p$ gives
\[
u^{[k]}(t,\hbar)=\int_0^t(t-\tau)e^{-(t-\tau)}R_k(\tau)\,d\tau,
\qquad k\ge1,
\]
where
\[
R_1=-\hbar F^{[0]},\qquad
R_k=(1+\hbar)\mathcal{L}_1[u^{[k-1]}]-\hbar F^{[k-1]},\quad k\ge2.
\]
For $t\ge0$ we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:28}
|u^{[0]}(t)|\le |u_0|+\frac{|v_0|}{e}=:U_0,
\qquad
|\dot u^{[0]}(t)|\le |v_0-u_0|+\frac{|v_0|}{e}=:V_0.
\end{equation}
It is further assumed that $U_0<r_1$, $V_0<r_2$. For fixed $\hbar$ set
\[
M_k=\|u^{[k]}\|_\infty,
\qquad
N_k=\|\dot u^{[k]}\|_\infty,
\qquad
\rho_k=\|R_k\|_\infty,
\qquad k\ge1.
\]

From \eqref{eq:26} it follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:29}
M_k\le\rho_k,\qquad N_k\le2\rho_k,\qquad k\ge1.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
U=u^{[0]}+\xi_1,\qquad \dot U=\dot u^{[0]}+\eta_1,
\]
where
\[
\xi_1=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}u^{[k]}(t,\hbar)p^k,
\qquad
\eta_1=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dot u^{[k]}(t,\hbar)p^k.
\]
Define
\[
\widetilde f(U,V)=\sum_{\mathfrak n,\mathfrak m\ge0}
|a_{\mathfrak n,\mathfrak m}|U^{\mathfrak n}V^{\mathfrak m},
\qquad
\Psi(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k z^k.
\]
Then
\[
\widehat F(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\widehat F^{[k]}z^k
\preceq
\widetilde f(U_0+\Psi(z),V_0+2\Psi(z)),
\]
where
\[
\widehat F^{[k]}=\sup_{t\ge0}|F^{[k]}(t,\hbar)|.
\]
Let $-2<\hbar<0$,
\[
\kappa=\frac{|\hbar|}{1-\upsilon},
\]
and
\[
\widetilde T(V)=\kappa\widetilde f(U_0+V,V_0+2V),
\qquad
V_{\max}=\min\left\{r_1-U_0,\frac{r_2-V_0}{2}\right\}.
\]

\begin{lemma}
If there exists $V^*\in(0,V_{\max})$, for which
\[
\widetilde T(V^*)\le V^*,
\]
then
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k\le V^*.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set
\[
S_m=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\rho_k,\qquad S_0=0.
\]
From the recurrence estimates we have
\[
S_m\le\upsilon S_{m-1}+|\hbar|\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\widehat F^{[k]}.
\]
The coefficientwise majorant for $\widehat F$ and the non-negativity of the coefficients of $\widetilde f$ give, for $S_{m-1}\le V^*$,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\widehat F^{[k]}
\le\widetilde f(U_0+V^*,V_0+2V^*).
\]
Hence $S_m\le V^*$. By induction, $S_m\le V^*$ for all $m\ge1$. Passing to the limit as $m\to\infty$, gives the required inequality.
\end{proof}

For $A\in(0,V_{\max})$ denote
\[
\zeta_A=\kappa\left[
\widetilde f_U(U_0+A,V_0+2A)+
2\widetilde f_V(U_0+A,V_0+2A)
\right].
\]

\begin{theorem}
Let $-2<\hbar<0$ and suppose there exists $A\in(0,V_{\max})$, for which
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:30}
\zeta_A<1,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:31}
\kappa\widetilde f(U_0,V_0)\le(1-\zeta_A)A.
\end{equation}
Then, at $p=1$ series \eqref{eq:27}, together with the series of its first and second derivatives, converges absolutely and uniformly on $[0,+\infty)$, and the sum of the series is the unique solution of problem \eqref{eq:24}, \eqref{eq:25}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
From conditions \eqref{eq:30}, \eqref{eq:31} we obtain $\widetilde T(A)\le A$. By Lemma~11,
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k<\infty.
\]
From \eqref{eq:29} and
\[
\ddot u^{[k]}=R_k-2\dot u^{[k]}-u^{[k]},\qquad k\ge1,
\]
we get
\[
\|\ddot u^{[k]}\|_\infty\le6\rho_k,
\]
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|F^{[k]}\|_\infty
\le\widetilde f(U_0+A,V_0+2A)<\infty,
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}F^{[k]}=f(u,\dot u).
\]
Passing to the limit in the recurrence equations gives
\[
\mathcal{L}_1[u]=(1+\hbar)\mathcal{L}_1[u]-\hbar f(u,\dot u),
\]
whence $\mathcal{L}_1[u]=f(u,\dot u)$ for $\hbar\ne0$. The initial conditions hold by construction, and uniqueness follows from the analyticity of $f$.
\end{proof}

For $-1\le\hbar<0$ we have $\kappa=1$, whereas for $-2<\hbar<-1$ we have $\kappa>1$. Hence, within this majorant estimate, the interval $[-1,0)$ gives the least restrictive sufficient conditions for convergence.

For problem \eqref{eq:22},
\[
f(u,\dot u)=-u\dot u-u^2,
\qquad
\widetilde f(U,V)=UV+U^2
\]
we have
\[
F^{[k]}=-\sum_{j=0}^{k}u^{[j]}
\left(\dot u^{[k-j]}+u^{[k-j]}\right).
\]
The first terms of the series have the form
\[
u^{[0]}(t)=(u_0+v_0t)e^{-t},
\]
\[
u^{[1]}(t,\hbar)=\hbar v_0\left[P(t)e^{-t}+Q(t)e^{-2t}\right],
\]
where
\[
P(t)=-u_0-2v_0+(u_0+v_0)t,
\qquad
Q(t)=u_0+2v_0+v_0t.
\]
Set
\[
c_2=-\frac{2u_0^2+6u_0v_0+3v_0^2}{4},
\qquad
c_3=\frac{6u_0^2+28u_0v_0+17v_0^2}{8},
\]
\[
D_1(t)=u_0^2+4u_0v_0+2v_0^2+2v_0(u_0+v_0)t,
\]
\[
K_1(t)=\frac{2u_0^2+4u_0v_0-v_0^2}{8}
+\frac{u_0v_0+v_0^2}{2}t+\frac{v_0^2}{4}t^2,
\]
\[
A_2(t)=(1+\hbar)\hbar v_0P(t)-\hbar^2v_0(c_3+c_2t),
\]
\[
A_3(t)=(1+\hbar)\hbar v_0Q(t)+\hbar^2v_0D_1(t).
\]
Then
\[
u^{[2]}(t,\hbar)=A_2(t)e^{-t}+A_3(t)e^{-2t}
-\hbar^2v_0K_1(t)e^{-3t}.
\]
For $-1\le\hbar<0$ conditions \eqref{eq:30}, \eqref{eq:31} take the form
\[
4U_0+V_0+6A<1,
\]
\[
U_0V_0+U_0^2\le[1-4U_0-V_0-6A]A.
\]
Setting
\[
a_2=1-4U_0-V_0,
\qquad
a_3=24(U_0V_0+U_0^2),
\]
for $a_2>0$, $a_2^2\ge a_3>0$ we obtain
\[
A\in\left[
\frac{a_2-\sqrt{a_2^2-a_3}}{12},
\frac{a_2+\sqrt{a_2^2-a_3}}{12}
\right]\cap(0,V_{\max}).
\]
In the case under consideration $V_{\max}=+\infty$. For $U_0=V_0=0$ we have the trivial solution $u(t)\equiv0$.

Thus the Cauchy problem for system \eqref{eq:20}, under the stated conditions, admits a convergent homotopy representation of its solution on $[0,+\infty)$.

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the Cauchy problem for system \eqref{eq:21} with
\[
u_0=-0.05,\qquad v_0=-0.03.
\]
From \eqref{eq:28} we have
\[
U_0\approx0.0610363832,\qquad V_0\approx0.0310363832.
\]
From conditions \eqref{eq:30}, \eqref{eq:31} we obtain
\[
\hbar_{\min}\le\hbar<0,
\qquad
\hbar_{\min}\approx-1.21770410.
\]
For each fixed $\hbar$ from this interval, the homotopy series of problem \eqref{eq:22}, \eqref{eq:23}, together with the series of its first and second derivatives, converges absolutely and uniformly on $[0,+\infty)$.

For a practical choice of $\hbar$ consider the second-order approximation
\[
u_2(t,\hbar)=u^{[0]}(t)+u^{[1]}(t,\hbar)+u^{[2]}(t,\hbar)
\]
and set, at $t=1$,
\[
\Psi_1(\hbar)=u_2(1,\hbar),
\]
and additionally consider
\[
\Psi_2(\hbar)=\left.\frac{\partial u_2(t,\hbar)}{\partial t}\right|_{t=1}.
\]
The functions $\Psi_1(\hbar)$, $\Psi_2(\hbar)$ attain their minima, respectively, at
\[
\hbar_{\Psi_1}^*\approx-1.015527,
\qquad
\hbar_{\Psi_2}^*\approx-1.032126.
\]
For $-1.231<\hbar<-0.739$ their values, rounded to four decimal places, equal $-0.0297$ and $0.0182$ respectively. Taking into account the conditions of Theorem~3, we choose the working interval
\[
\hbar_{\min}\le\hbar<-0.739.
\]

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.58\textwidth]{figure3.png}
\caption{The $\hbar$-curve $\Psi_1(\hbar)=u_2(1,\hbar)$, obtained at the second order of approximation. The working interval $[\hbar_{\min},-0.739)$ is highlighted.}
\label{fig:hcurve}
\end{figure}

For $\hbar=-1$ the second-order approximation has the form
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_2(t,-1)\approx{}&-(0.046428875+0.03252525t)e^{-t}\\
&-(0.003609+0.001044t)e^{-2t}\\
&+(0.000037875+0.000036t+0.00000675t^2)e^{-3t}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The original variables are recovered from the formulas
\[
x_1(t)\approx1+u_2(t,-1),
\qquad
y_1(t)\approx1+u_2(t,-1)+\dot u_2(t,-1).
\]
Figure~\ref{fig:numcomp} shows their comparison with the numerical solutions $X_1,Y_1$ of system \eqref{eq:20}, obtained using MathCAD with initial conditions $x_1(0)=0.95$, $y_1(0)=0.97$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{figure4.png}
\caption{Graphs of the numerical and approximate analytical solutions of system \eqref{eq:20}.}
\label{fig:numcomp}
\end{figure}

In the numerical comparison on the interval $[0,7]$ the absolute discrepancy for both components is less than $2.2402\cdot10^{-7}$. On the interval $(7,25]$ it does not exceed $2.3290\cdot10^{-8}$.

title: Example
body_md:
We study the Cauchy problem for the continuous analogue of $W_1$ \cite{ref10}. On $\Omega_2$ the system has the form
\[
\begin{cases}
\dot x_1=x_2y_1,\\
\dot x_2=x_2y_2-x_2,\\
\dot y_1=x_1+x_2y_1-y_1,\\
\dot y_2=x_2y_2-y_2,
\end{cases}
\quad
(x_1(0),x_2(0),y_1(0),y_2(0))=(x_1^0,x_2^0,y_1^0,y_2^0)\in\Omega_2.
\]
For this problem an exact analytical solution was obtained in \cite{ref26}.

Taking into account the simplex conditions, we get
\[
x_2(t)-y_2(t)=c_4e^{-t},
\qquad c_4=x_2^0-y_2^0.
\]
Consequently, $y_2$ satisfies the Riccati equation
\[
\dot y_2+(1-c_4e^{-t})y_2-y_2^2=0,
\qquad y_2(0)=y_2^0.
\]
Set
\[
\mathcal{L}_2[\varphi]=\dot\varphi+(1-c_4e^{-t})\varphi,
\qquad
E_2(t)=\exp[-t+c_4(1-e^{-t})].
\]
At $\hbar=-1$ the deformation equation takes the form
\[
\mathcal{L}_2[Y_2]=pY_2^2,
\qquad Y_2(0,p)=y_2^0.
\]
\[
Y_2(t,p)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}y_2^{[k]}(t)p^k,
\qquad y_2^{[0]}(t)=y_2^0E_2(t),
\]
and the recurrence equations have the form
\[
\mathcal{L}_2[y_2^{[k]}]
=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}y_2^{[j]}y_2^{[k-1-j]},
\qquad y_2^{[k]}(0)=0,\quad k\ge1.
\]
Denote
\[
I_3(t)=\int_0^tE_2(s)\,ds
=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\exp[c_4(1-e^{-t})]-1}{c_4},&c_4\ne0,\\[2ex]
1-e^{-t},&c_4=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Since
\[
\mathcal{L}_2[E_2(t)I_3^k(t)]=kE_2^2(t)I_3^{k-1}(t),\qquad k\ge1,
\]
by induction
\[
y_2^{[k]}(t)=(y_2^0)^{k+1}E_2(t)I_3^k(t),
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.
\]
For interior initial data,
\[
E_2(t)\le e^{-[1-\max\{c_4,0\}]t},
\qquad
\sup_{t\ge0}y_2^0I_3(t)
\le\frac{y_2^0}{1-\max\{c_4,0\}}<1.
\]
Hence, for $p=1$ the geometric series converges absolutely and uniformly on $[0,+\infty)$, and
\[
y_2(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}y_2^{[k]}(t)
=\frac{y_2^0E_2(t)}{1-y_2^0I_3(t)}.
\]
The remaining components are recovered from the equalities
\[
x_2(t)=y_2(t)+c_4e^{-t},
\qquad x_1(t)=1-x_2(t),
\qquad y_1(t)=1-y_2(t).
\]
This formula coincides with the corresponding exact solution from \cite{ref26}.

An analogous construction at $\hbar=-1$ applies to the problem
\[
\dot u(t)+f_1(t)u(t)-\beta_1u^2(t)=0,
\qquad u(0)=u_0,
\]
where
\[
f_1(t)\in C[0,T],\qquad \beta_1,u_0\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Set
\[
E_3(t)=\exp\left(-\int_0^t f_1(s)\,ds\right),
\qquad
I_4(t)=\int_0^tE_3(s)\,ds.
\]
If
\[
|\beta_1u_0|I_4(T)<1,
\]
then the homotopy series converges uniformly on $[0,T]$, and its sum equals
\[
u(t)=\frac{u_0E_3(t)}{1-\beta_1u_0I_4(t)}.
\]
